newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Welfare to hit back in Islamist row.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Welfare to hit back in Islamist row.

text.p: Turkey's ruling Islamists on Thursday vowed to hit back at efforts to outlaw them in a row with the secularist establishment that has deadlocked the government and damaged Turkey's standing abroad.
A close aide to Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan said the Islamists would take legal action against the country's top prosecutor for attempting to close their Welfare Party.
"We will bring him to court. He produced unlawful and groundless documents against us," State Minister Abdullah Gul told Reuters in an interview.
Prosecutor Vural Savas on Wednesday filed a case with the constitutional court to ban Welfare for allegedly endangering the secularist pillars of the Turkish state.
But Gul predicted that the Islamists would survive the threat because they had abided by the rules of democracy.
"There is no way that in a democracy they can close political parties if they have not been involved in violence, in unlawful actions such as force or terror," he said.
Last June, Erbakan became the first Islamist to lead the Turks since the collapse of the Ottoman Empire, after he narrowly won general polls with 21 percent of the vote.
He has since angered secularists who say he has no mandate for his efforts to increase the role of Islam in public life.
Welfare's coalition with a pro-Western party has been hamstrung by squabbling over religious activism between the Islamists and influential security officials.
Istanbul stocks dived 2.52 percent at the close on Thursday on political uncertainties, brokers said.
The cabinet is to meet later for the first time in seven weeks. It will be minus three anti-Islamist ministers who have quit in the interlude in protest at Erbakan.
Anatolian news agency said Ankara's governor had asked residents of the capital to help enforce a ban on Islamic-style dress as part of military-inspired curbs on religious activism.
"Inform the governor's office if you see anyone who does not comply with the dress law by wearing robes and turbans on Ankara streets," governor Erdogan Sahinoglu told the agency.
Erbakan has stalled on army demands to lead the crackdown.

The Turkish press this week quoted an unnamed general as saying the army distrusted the Islamists so much that it did not tell the cabinet in advance of a large cross-border operation into Iraq after Kurdish rebels that began last week.

Iraqi Kurdish officials said Turkish troops had pushed 200 km (125 miles) into northern Iraq, much further than during past incursions. This follows reports at home and abroad that Iraq, Syria and Iran have all built up forces in the region.
Promises by Welfare to solve a 12-year-old Kurdish separatist insurgency in southeast Turkey through "Moslem brotherhood" have been quietly forgotten in recent months.
Turkey has not had a stable government since Tansu Ciller, now the foreign minister, resigned as prime minister in 1995.
Commentator Mehmet Ali Birand said the domestic uncertainty was hurting Turkey's bid to be a full member of the West at a time the European Union and NATO were expanding.
"The political confusion is damaging," he wrote in the Sabah daily. "These developments involve us closely but Turkey is not on the stage," he said.
